title: Close the Loop Before You Start the Next One
summary: Before jumping to the next task, spend five minutes on the last one: what changed, how you know, what is left. It helps the next person, your planning and your own focus.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Friday, 4 p.m. The PR merged an hour ago, the ticket says Done, and the next task is already waiting in your queue with a "high priority" label. It's tempting to just open it. But nobody has written down what changed, how you checked it, or what the next person should know before touching that part of the code. That next person might be you, three weeks from now.

Most teams are great at opening loops: kickoffs, tickets, branches, spikes, experiments. Starting feels good and shows progress right away. Closing pays off later, and usually for someone else, so it's the step that gets skipped when the next thing starts pulling.

What a closed loop looks like

A piece of work is closed when it leaves behind something another person can use. In practice that means a handful of answers:

  • What changed, or what did we decide?
  • How do we know it works? Which test, which dashboard, which check?
  • What did we learn that we didn't know at the start?
  • What's still risky, and what did we leave out on purpose?
  • Who owns the follow-up, and when do we look again?

Scrum has a version of this built in. The Scrum Guide calls the Definition of Done "a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product," and says it "creates transparency by providing everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed" (The Scrum Guide 2020). A closing note does the same job for what the Definition of Done doesn't cover: the decisions, the caveats, the things still sitting in someone's head.

Why it's worth five minutes

The first reason is the next person. Teams rarely revisit a tidy past. They revisit fragments: a support ticket that touches old behavior, a regression in code nobody has opened for months, a new teammate asking why some odd constraint exists. If the loop wasn't closed, someone pays to rebuild the context later, usually under more pressure. Google's SRE book makes the point about incidents: "Unless we have some formalized process of learning from these incidents in place, they may recur ad infinitum" (Postmortem Culture). Everyday work runs on the same logic, with lower stakes.

The second reason is you. Sophie Leroy, then at the University of Washington Bothell's School of Business, studies what she calls attention residue: still thinking about the last task when you need to focus on the next one. In a 2018 paper with Theresa Glomb, people who wrote a quick "ready-to-resume" plan before switching (where they left off, what challenges remained, what they had to postpone) made better decisions and recalled more on the task that followed (UW News; Organization Science, 2018). The plan "needn't be long or elaborate." Leroy compared unfinished work to windows left open in your head.

That research was about interrupted tasks, not finished ones. Still, I find the same trick works for work that's "done, but not quite": write down where it stands, and it gets easier to give the next task your full attention.

The third reason is planning. When loops close well, the team can see where work actually ended, which assumptions held and which follow-ups are still open. Estimates for the next round get less foggy because they start from a written record.

Close it where people will look

Closing doesn't need a ceremony or a new tool. It needs a few traces in the places future work will pass through:

  • The PR description ends with how you verified it: the test command, a screenshot, the dashboard you checked after deploy.
  • The ticket gets the live URL, the release version and anything you decided not to do.
  • The meeting note links to the decision, so nobody has to dig it out of chat (more on keeping notes close to decisions).
  • The rollout note says what would trigger a rollback and who's watching for it.
  • The handoff says what's known, what isn't and what was left out on purpose (making handoffs easier to receive).

Good closing notes are factual and a little boring. Skip the victory lap and the vague "should be fine." Write what someone can use: the commit that shipped, the test result, the known caveat, the owner, the next check.

A closing note in four lines

Changed: checkout retries now back off for up to 30 seconds.
Verified: load test on staging, plus the error-rate graph after deploy.
Still open: the mobile app keeps the old client until its next release.
Owner: Linh checks the retry dashboard again on Monday.

Finish before you start

Loops are easier to close when fewer are open at once. The Kanban Guide defines work in progress as "the number of work items started but not finished" and says teams "must explicitly control" it (The Kanban Guide). It adds that controlling WIP "often improves the Kanban system members' collective focus, commitment, and collaboration." With five tickets all at "almost done," closing any one of them properly feels like a luxury. With two, it's just part of the job. If your team is still choosing how to run its board, here's a look at Kanban vs. Scrum.

Try this week

  • Before you pick up your next ticket, write three lines on the last one: what changed, how you know, what's left.
  • Add a "How I verified this" section to your PR template.
  • Count the items on your board that are "almost done." Close one properly before starting anything new.
  • At the end of your next meeting, spend two minutes writing the decision and its owner where the team will find them.

Often one sentence is enough: here's what changed, here's how we know, here's what's left. Then the next task feels like a continuation instead of a restart.

faqs.q: What does closing the loop mean at work?
faqs.a: It means leaving a short, findable record when a piece of work ends: what changed or was decided, how you verified it, what is still risky or deliberately left out, and who owns the follow-up. The work isn't fully done until someone else could pick it up from that record.

faqs.q: What should a closing note include?
faqs.a: Keep it factual: the commit or release that shipped, how you checked it (test, dashboard, screenshot), known caveats, what you chose not to do, the owner of any follow-up and when it gets checked again. Put it where people will look, such as the PR, the ticket or the meeting note.

faqs.q: Isn't the Definition of Done enough?
faqs.a: The Scrum Guide's Definition of Done gives everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed and the quality bar it met. A closing note covers what it usually doesn't: the decisions made along the way, the caveats and the follow-ups still open.

faqs.q: Does writing a quick note before switching tasks help focus?
faqs.a: Research suggests it can. Sophie Leroy and Theresa Glomb (Organization Science, 2018) found that people who wrote a brief ready-to-resume plan before switching away from an interrupted task made better decisions and recalled more on the next task. Their studies covered interrupted tasks, and the plan took about a minute.
